statement: An ideal 24 V source feeds a divider made of R1 = 4.7 kΩ (source to node OUT) and R2 = 10 kΩ (OUT to ground). A 22 kΩ load RL is connected from OUT to ground as well. Find the voltage at OUT in volts.
solution: 1. The load is in parallel with R2: R2 || RL = 6875 ohm. 2. Now it is a plain divider: Vout = 24 * 6875 / (4700 + 6875). 3. Vout = 14.25 V.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ignored the load and used R2 alone as the lower resistor
common_mistakes.why: RL draws current, so the lower leg is R2 || RL, not R2.

common_mistakes.mistake: Added R2 and RL in series (R2 + RL) for the lower leg
common_mistakes.why: Both resistors connect OUT to ground, so they are in parallel.

criteria.text: Combines R2 and RL as a parallel pair
Applies the divider ratio with the combined lower resistance

statement: 15 mA flows into a node and leaves to ground through three resistors in parallel: 1 kΩ, 2.2 kΩ and 3.3 kΩ. How much of it goes through the 2.2 kΩ resistor? Give the answer in mA.
solution: 1. Current splits in proportion to conductance. G1 = 1/1000, G2 = 1/2200, G3 = 1/3300 siemens. 2. Total conductance = 0.0017576 S, and G2 = 0.00045455 S. 3. I2 = 15 mA * G2 / Gtotal = 3.879 mA.

common_mistakes.mistake: Split the current in proportion to resistance instead of conductance
common_mistakes.why: More current takes the lower resistance; the share is proportional to G, not R.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treated it as a two-resistor divider using only the 1 kΩ and 2.2 kΩ
common_mistakes.why: The third branch also takes current; ignoring it overestimates every other branch.

criteria.text: Uses conductances (or parallel equivalent of the other branches) for the split
Includes all three branches in the total

statement: A bridge is fed by an ideal 12 V source between node P (positive) and ground. Left arm: R1 = 1.2 kΩ from P to A, R2 = 1.8 kΩ from A to ground. Right arm: R3 = 2.7 kΩ from P to B, R4 = 2.2 kΩ from B to ground. A detector with Rg = 470 Ω sits between A and B. What current flows through the detector? Take A to B as positive and answer in microamperes.
solution: 1. Open-circuit voltage between A and B: vA = 12*1800/(1200+1800) = 7.2 V, vB = 12*2200/(2700+2200) = 5.388 V, so Vth = 1.812 V. 2. Resistance seen from A and B with the source shorted: (1200 || 1800) + (2700 || 2200) = 1932 ohm. 3. Detector current = Vth / (Rth + Rg) = 1.812 / (1932 + 470) = 754.4 uA, from A to B (vA > vB).

common_mistakes.mistake: Divided the open-circuit voltage by Rg alone
common_mistakes.why: The bridge resistors are in the loop; the detector sees Rth + Rg.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reported the current with the wrong sign (B to A)
common_mistakes.why: vA is higher than vB, so the current flows from A to B.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used Vth / Rth and left out the detector resistance
common_mistakes.why: The detector is part of the loop and adds to the resistance.

criteria.text: Finds the A-B open-circuit voltage from the two dividers
Finds the Thevenin resistance with the source set to zero
Adds the detector resistance in the final division

statement: A quarter bridge runs from a 5 V supply, positive at node P and negative at ground. One leg is two 120 Ω resistors in series from P to ground, meeting at A. The other leg has a fixed 120 Ω resistor from P to B and a strain gauge from B to ground. Under strain the gauge has gone from 120 Ω to 126 Ω. Calculate v(B) - v(A) in millivolts. Work it out exactly, without the small-change approximation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used the small-change formula V*dR/(4R)
common_mistakes.why: dR/R = 5 % is not small enough for 1 % accuracy; the exact result is smaller.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used V*dR/R, forgetting the factor of 4 in the quarter-bridge approximation
common_mistakes.why: Only one arm changes and the bridge halves the divider voltage, giving dR/(4R).

criteria.text: Uses the exact ratio, not the approximation

statement: Three branches meet at node X. R1 = 4 Ω runs from X to node N1, which an ideal source holds at +12 V relative to ground. R2 = 6 Ω runs from X to node N2, and an ideal 5 V source sits between N2 and ground with its positive terminal on ground and its negative terminal on N2. The third branch is R3 = 12 Ω from X to ground. Use superposition to find the voltage at X, in volts.
solution: 1. Source 1 alone (source 2 shorted): R2 || R3 = 4 ohm, so vX = 12 * 4 / (4 + 4) = 6 V. 2. Source 2 alone: N2 is at -5 V. R1 || R3 = 3 ohm, so vX = -5 * 3 / (6 + 3) = -1.667 V. 3. Add: vX = 6 + (-1.667) = 4.333 V.

common_mistakes.mistake: Took the 5 V source as +5 V at N2
common_mistakes.why: Positive terminal is at ground, so N2 sits at -5 V relative to ground.

common_mistakes.mistake: Kept the other source's resistance out when shorting (used R3 alone as the lower leg)
common_mistakes.why: A shorted voltage source leaves its series resistor in the circuit, in parallel with R3 from X's point of view.

criteria.text: Handles the polarity of source 2 (N2 at -5 V)
Shorts the inactive voltage source correctly in each step

statement: R3 = 10 Ω connects node X to ground. X is also tied to node N1 through R1 = 5 Ω and to node N2 through R2 = 20 Ω. Ideal sources hold N1 at +10 V and N2 at +6 V, both relative to ground. With both sources active, how much power does R3 dissipate, in watts?
solution: 1. Power is quadratic, so superposition applies to the voltage (or current), not to power. 2. Source 1 alone gives vX = 5.714 V; source 2 alone gives 0.8571 V; total vX = 6.571 V. 3. P(R3) = vX^2 / R3 = 6.571^2 / 10 = 4.318 W.

common_mistakes.mistake: Added the powers computed for each source separately
common_mistakes.why: P = v^2/R is not linear: the cross term 2*v1*v2/R is missing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used the sum of the source voltages across R3
common_mistakes.why: The sources are divided by R1 and R2 before they reach R3.

criteria.text: Finds the total node voltage first (by superposition or node equation)
Squares the total voltage, does not add powers

statement: Node C is held at +9 V relative to ground by an ideal source. R1 = 3 kΩ goes from C to node A, R2 = 6 kΩ from A to ground, R3 = 2 kΩ from A to node B, and R4 = 4 kΩ from B to ground. An ideal current source takes 2 mA from ground and pushes it into B. Use node analysis to get the voltage at B, in volts.
solution: 1. KCL at A (conductances in mS): (1/3 + 1/6 + 1/2) vA - (1/2) vB = 9/3, i.e. 1.0 vA - 0.5 vB = 3. 2. KCL at B: -(1/2) vA + (1/2 + 1/4) vB = 2, i.e. -0.5 vA + 0.75 vB = 2. 3. Solve the pair: vA = 6.5 V and vB = 7 V.

common_mistakes.mistake: Left the current source out of the node B equation
common_mistakes.why: The source injects current into B and must appear on the right-hand side of the KCL at B.

common_mistakes.mistake: Entered the current source with the wrong sign
common_mistakes.why: It pushes current into B, so it adds +2 mA to the current balance there.

criteria.text: Writes the node equation at A correctly
Writes the node equation at B with the current source sign right

statement: Node X is the junction of three branches. The first is an ideal 24 V source in series with 6 Ω, the second an ideal 5 V source in series with 4 Ω; in both, the positive terminal faces X and the negative terminal is at ground. The third branch is 3 Ω from X to ground. What current does the 5 V source deliver to node X through its branch, in amperes? Count it positive if it flows out of the positive terminal toward X, and negative if it flows into the positive terminal.
solution: 1. Node equation at X: (24 - vX)/6 + (5 - vX)/4 = vX/3. 2. Multiply by 12: 2(24 - vX) + 3(5 - vX) = 4 vX, so 9 vX = 63 and vX = 7 V. 3. Current out of the 5 V source's positive terminal = (5 - 7)/4 = -0.5 A. The negative sign means current actually flows into that source: the 24 V branch is charging it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Gave the magnitude only (+0.5 A)
common_mistakes.why: vX (7 V) is higher than the 5 V source, so current flows into its positive terminal.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assumed the 5 V source delivers power because it is a source
common_mistakes.why: A source absorbs power when current enters its positive terminal; check the sign of the branch current.

criteria.text: Writes the KCL at X with all three branches
States the sign and direction of the branch current

statement: A resistor ladder runs from terminal A to ground, with no sources connected: R1 = 120 Ω from A to node M, R2 = 240 Ω from M to ground, R3 = 60 Ω from M to node K, R4 = 150 Ω from K to ground. What is the resistance between A and ground, in ohms?
solution: 1. Work from the far end. R3 and R4 are in series: 210 ohm. 2. That pair is in parallel with R2: 240 || 210 = 112 ohm. 3. R1 is in series with the result: 120 + 112 = 232 ohm.

common_mistakes.mistake: Added all four resistors in series
common_mistakes.why: R2 and R4 return to ground, so they are shunts, not series elements.

common_mistakes.mistake: Put R3 in parallel with R2 instead of in series with R4
common_mistakes.why: R3 and R4 form one branch to ground; K is not a source terminal.

criteria.text: Starts from the end remote from the terminals
Identifies series R3+R4 and its parallel with R2
Adds R1 in series at the end

statement: Five resistors form a bridge between terminals A and B: R1 = 10 Ω (A to C), R2 = 30 Ω (A to D), R3 = 40 Ω (C to B), R4 = 20 Ω (D to B), and R5 = 15 Ω across the middle from C to D. Find the equivalent resistance between A and B in ohms.
solution: 1. The bridge is not balanced and has no series/parallel pairs. Convert the delta A-C-D (R1, R2, R5) into a wye. Sum = 55 ohm. 2. Wye arms: Ra = R1*R2/sum = 5.455, Rc = R1*R5/sum = 2.727, Rd = R2*R5/sum = 8.182 ohm (each arm is the product of the two delta resistors touching that corner, over the sum). 3. Now two paths to B: Rc + R3 = 42.73 and Rd + R4 = 28.18 ohm in parallel = 16.98 ohm. 4. Req = Ra + 16.98 = 22.44 ohm.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ignored R5 (treated the bridge as two parallel series paths)
common_mistakes.why: R5 carries current because the bridge is not balanced (R1*R4 differs from R2*R3).

common_mistakes.mistake: Replaced R5 by a short circuit
common_mistakes.why: A short is only correct if R5 = 0; here it is 15 ohm.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used delta-wye arms as the sum of the neighbouring resistors
common_mistakes.why: Each wye arm is a product over the sum of the three delta resistors, not a sum.

criteria.text: Recognises the need for a delta-wye conversion (or writes node equations)
Computes the three wye arms with product/sum
Combines the series and parallel paths afterwards

statement: In this network an ideal 24 V source sits between node N1 (positive) and ground, R1 = 6 kΩ connects N1 to terminal A, and R2 = 12 kΩ connects A to ground. An ideal current source also pushes 2 mA from ground into A. What is the Thevenin (open-circuit) voltage between A and ground? Answer in volts.
solution: 1. Superposition with A open. Voltage source alone: vA = 24*12000/(6000+12000) = 16 V. 2. Current source alone (voltage source shorted): the 2 mA flows through R1 || R2 = 4000 ohm, giving 8 V. 3. Add them: Vth = 24 V.

common_mistakes.mistake: Left out the current source
common_mistakes.why: The current source still pushes current into A and raises its voltage.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used only the current source's contribution
common_mistakes.why: The voltage source also contributes through the R1/R2 divider.

criteria.text: Treats each source separately (or writes the node equation) with the other set to zero
Includes the current source contribution through R1 || R2

statement: An ideal 18 V source connects node N1 (positive) to ground. R1 = 3 kΩ goes from N1 to node A, R2 = 6 kΩ from A to ground, R3 = 2 kΩ from A to terminal B, and R4 = 4 kΩ from B to ground. The output port is B and ground. Find the Norton (short-circuit) current of the port, taken as flowing from B to ground through the short, in milliamperes.
solution: 1. Short B to ground. R4 is then bypassed and carries no current. 2. R2 || R3 = 1500 ohm, so vA = 18*1500/(3000+1500) = 6 V. 3. The short-circuit current flows through R3: I_N = vA / R3 = 3 mA.

common_mistakes.mistake: Divided the open-circuit voltage at B by R4
common_mistakes.why: With the port shorted R4 is bypassed; the open-circuit voltage is not the voltage during the short.

common_mistakes.mistake: Left R2 out of the short-circuit calculation
common_mistakes.why: R2 still loads node A; it is in parallel with the path through the short.

criteria.text: Shorts the port and notes R4 carries no current
Finds the node A voltage with R2 and R3 in parallel
Divides by R3 for the short-circuit current

statement: An ideal 24 V source sits between node N1 (positive) and ground. R1 = 6 kΩ connects N1 to terminal A, R2 = 12 kΩ connects A to ground, and an ideal current source pushes 2 mA into A from ground. A variable resistor is placed between A and ground. As its resistance is varied, what is the most power it can receive? Give it in milliwatts.
solution: 1. Thevenin voltage at A: Vth = 24 V (voltage source 16 V plus current source 8 V). 2. Thevenin resistance with both sources set to zero (current source open): R1 || R2 = 4000 ohm. 3. Maximum power occurs for RL = Rth = 4000 ohm: Pmax = Vth^2/(4 Rth) = 576/16000 = 36 mW.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used Vth^2/Rth, leaving out the factor 4
common_mistakes.why: At matching the load sees only half of Vth, and the load power is Vth^2/(4 Rth).

common_mistakes.mistake: Used only the voltage source's 16 V as Vth
common_mistakes.why: The current source contributes 8 V to the open-circuit voltage.

criteria.text: Finds Vth including the current source
Finds Rth with the current source open-circuited
Sets RL = Rth and uses Vth^2/(4 Rth)

statement: An AC source has an open-circuit voltage of 120 V RMS and a Thevenin impedance of 30 + j40 ohm. Both the resistance and the reactance of the load can be chosen freely. What is the maximum average power the load can receive, in watts?
solution: 1. For a freely chosen load, the optimum is the complex conjugate: ZL = 30 - j40 ohm, which cancels the reactance. 2. The total loop resistance is 2*30 = 60 ohm and the RMS current is 120/60 = 2 A. 3. Load power = I^2 * 30 = Vrms^2/(4 Rth) = 120 W.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used the peak-value formula V^2/(8 R) with an RMS voltage
common_mistakes.why: V^2/(8R) belongs to peak amplitude; with RMS the factor is 4.

criteria.text: Notes the reactances cancel and only resistance limits the current

statement: A source with a Thevenin impedance of 30 + j40 ohm has an open-circuit voltage of 120 V RMS. The load has to be a pure resistance, adjustable anywhere from 1 ohm to 1 kilohm. Find the largest average power the load can receive, in watts.
solution: 1. With a resistive load the reactance cannot be cancelled. Power in R: P = Vrms^2 R / ((Rth + R)^2 + Xth^2). 2. Setting dP/dR = 0 gives R = sqrt(Rth^2 + Xth^2) = |Zth| = 50 ohm (inside the allowed range). 3. P = 14400 * 50 / ((30+50)^2 + 40^2) = 90 W.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used the conjugate-match result (120 W)
common_mistakes.why: A pure resistor cannot supply the -j40 ohm needed for a conjugate match.

common_mistakes.mistake: Chose R = Rth = 30 ohm
common_mistakes.why: With a series reactance the best resistance is |Zth|, not Rth.

criteria.text: Chooses RL = |Zth| for a resistive load
Evaluates the power including Xth in the denominator
Checks the value lies in the allowed range

statement: An ideal 15 V source connects node N1 (positive) to ground. R1 = 100 Ω joins N1 to terminal A and R2 = 150 Ω joins A to ground. There is also a branch from A through R3 = 30 Ω to node N3, and an ideal current source pushes 40 mA from ground into N3. Find the Thevenin resistance seen between A and ground, in ohms.
solution: 1. Set independent sources to zero: the voltage source becomes a short, the current source becomes an open circuit. 2. The open current source leaves R3 dangling from A, so R3 carries no current and does not count. 3. Rth = R1 || R2 = 100 || 150 = 60 ohm.

common_mistakes.mistake: Replaced the current source by a short, putting R3 in parallel
common_mistakes.why: A zeroed current source is an open circuit, which removes the R3 branch.

common_mistakes.mistake: Opened the voltage source instead of shorting it
common_mistakes.why: A zeroed voltage source is a short, so R1 goes to ground.

criteria.text: Replaces the voltage source by a short
Replaces the current source by an open circuit

statement: An uncharged 22 µF capacitor is charged from a 9 V DC source through a 47 kΩ resistor. How many seconds after the switch closes does the capacitor voltage reach 6 V?

common_mistakes.mistake: Took t = tau because 6 V is 'about 63 %' of 9 V
common_mistakes.why: 6/9 is 66.7 %, not 63.2 %; the exact time is tau ln 3.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used the discharge form t = tau ln(Vs/Vt)
common_mistakes.why: That is the time to fall from 9 V to 6 V; charging to 6 V needs ln(Vs/(Vs - Vt)).

criteria.text: Computes tau = RC with correct kilo/micro scaling
Uses the charging equation with final value 9 V
Solves for t with the correct logarithm

statement: A 250 mH coil (treat it as ideal) in series with a 40 Ω resistor is switched onto a 24 V DC source at t = 0, starting from zero current. What is the current at t = 3 ms? Answer in mA.

common_mistakes.mistake: Gave the steady-state current
common_mistakes.why: At t = 3 ms the current has only reached about 38 % of its final value.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used L = 250 (not converting mH) in tau = L/R
common_mistakes.why: L = 250 mH = 0.25 H; mixing units makes tau a thousand times too large.

criteria.text: Computes tau = L/R with L in henries
Uses i = Ifinal(1 - e^(-t/tau)) with Ifinal = V/R

statement: An ideal 20 V source connects node IN to ground. R1 = 10 kΩ connects IN to node X, and both R2 = 15 kΩ and a 10 µF capacitor are connected from X to ground. The capacitor is uncharged when the source is switched on at t = 0. What is the capacitor voltage at t = 50 ms, in volts?
solution: 1. Look back into the capacitor terminals: Vth = 20*15000/(10000+15000) = 12 V and Rth = R1 || R2 = 6000 ohm. 2. The capacitor charges toward Vth with tau = Rth C = 6000 ohm * 10 uF = 60 ms. 3. vC(50 ms) = 12 (1 - e^(-50/60)) = 6.785 V.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used the full 20 V source as the final value
common_mistakes.why: R2 forms a divider with R1, so the capacitor settles at the Thevenin voltage of 12 V, not 20 V.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used tau = R1 C and final value 20 V
common_mistakes.why: The capacitor sees R1 || R2 as its charging resistance, and the final voltage is 12 V.

criteria.text: Finds the Thevenin voltage and resistance seen by the capacitor
Charges toward Vth, not the source voltage

statement: A 50 mH coil is carrying 2 A when its supply is disconnected; from then on a 10 Ω resistor closes the loop. The coil's own resistance is negligible. How many milliseconds does it take for the current to fall to 200 mA?
solution: 1. tau = L/R = 50 mH/10 ohm = 5 ms. 2. i(t) = 2 e^(-t/tau); set it equal to 0.2 A: e^(-t/tau) = 0.1. 3. t = tau ln(10) = 5 ms * 2.303 = 11.51 ms.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used 5 time constants as 'fully decayed'
common_mistakes.why: 5 tau gives 0.67 % of the initial value (13 mA), not 10 %.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used log base 10 instead of the natural log
common_mistakes.why: The exponential solution needs ln, so t = tau ln(10) = 2.303 tau.

criteria.text: Uses the decaying exponential with initial 2 A

statement: A 470 µF capacitor starts uncharged and is charged to 12 V through a resistor from an ideal 12 V DC source. Find the total energy the source delivers over the whole charging process, in millijoules.
solution: 1. The charge that moves through the source is Q = C V = 470 uF * 12 V = 5.64 mC. 2. The source holds 12 V the whole time, so it delivers E = Q V = C V^2 = 67.68 mJ. 3. Check: the capacitor stores C V^2/2 = 33.84 mJ and the resistor dissipates the other 33.84 mJ, whatever the resistance is.

common_mistakes.mistake: Gave the energy stored in the capacitor, C V^2/2
common_mistakes.why: That is only half of what the source supplies; the other half is lost as heat in the resistor.

criteria.text: Uses charge Q = CV moved through the source at constant voltage
Gets E = C V^2 (not C V^2/2)
Can account for the half stored and half dissipated

statement: An ideal 12 V source connects node N1 to ground. R1 = 4 Ω runs from N1 to node A. From A, R3 = 12 Ω goes to ground and R2 = 12 Ω goes to node B, and an ideal 100 mH inductor connects B to ground. The source is switched on at t = 0 with zero inductor current. Find the inductor current (from B to ground) at t = 10 ms, in milliamperes.
solution: 1. Look back into the inductor terminals: Vth = 12*12/(4+12) = 9 V, Rth = R2 + R1 || R3 = 12 + 3 = 15 ohm. 2. Final current = Vth/Rth = 0.6 A and tau = L/Rth = 0.1/15 = 6.667 ms. 3. i(10 ms) = 0.6 (1 - e^(-1.5)) = 0.4661 A = 466.1 mA.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used tau = L/R2 and ignored R1 || R3
common_mistakes.why: The source side presents R1 || R3 = 3 ohm in series with R2 to the inductor.

common_mistakes.mistake: Took the final current as 12/(4+12) = 0.75 A, ignoring R3, but kept tau = L/15 ohm
common_mistakes.why: R3 is a path to ground at A. It changes both the Thevenin voltage (9 V) and the final current (0.6 A).

criteria.text: Finds Vth and Rth seen by the inductor

statement: A 22 Ω resistor, a 15 mH inductor and a 33 µF capacitor are in series across a 50 Hz supply. What is the magnitude of the total impedance, in ohms?
solution: 1. Angular frequency w = 2 pi f = 314.2 rad/s. 2. XL = w L = 4.712 ohm and XC = 1/(w C) = 96.46 ohm; the net reactance is XL - XC = -91.75 ohm (capacitive). 3. |Z| = sqrt(R^2 + X^2) = sqrt(22^2 + 91.75^2) = 94.35 ohm.

common_mistakes.mistake: Added R, XL and XC arithmetically
common_mistakes.why: R, XL and XC are at 0, +90 and -90 degrees; they add as phasors, not as magnitudes.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used f in place of w when computing XL and XC
common_mistakes.why: Reactance needs w = 2 pi f in rad/s.

common_mistakes.mistake: Added XL and XC instead of subtracting
common_mistakes.why: The capacitor's reactance has the opposite sign to the inductor's.

criteria.text: Gets XL and XC and subtracts them
Combines R and net X in quadrature

statement: A 40 Ω resistor and a 150 mH inductor in series are connected to a 230 V RMS, 50 Hz source, with the source voltage as the 0 degree reference. What is the phase angle of the current phasor, in degrees? Use the convention that a lagging current has a negative angle.
solution: 1. XL = 2 pi f L = 47.12 ohm, so Z = 40 + j47.12 ohm. 2. The impedance angle is atan(XL/R) = atan(47.12/40) = 49.67 degrees. 3. I = V/Z, so the current angle is 0 - 49.67 = -49.67 degrees (the current lags the voltage).

common_mistakes.mistake: Reported the impedance angle with a positive sign
common_mistakes.why: The current angle is the source angle minus the impedance angle, so it is negative for an inductive load.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used atan(R/XL)
common_mistakes.why: The angle of Z is atan(X/R), the reactance over the resistance.

criteria.text: Takes atan(XL/R) for the impedance angle

statement: An RC low-pass filter has a 1 kΩ series resistor and a 100 nF capacitor to ground, with the output taken across the capacitor. It is driven by a 5 V peak sine wave at 2 kHz. Find the peak output voltage in volts.
solution: 1. w R C = 2 pi * 2000 Hz * 1000 ohm * 100 nF = 1.257. 2. The divider between R and the capacitor's impedance gives |H| = 1/sqrt(1 + (w R C)^2) = 0.6227. 3. Peak output = 5 * 0.6227 = 3.113 V.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used f instead of w in w R C
common_mistakes.why: The impedance of C is 1/(j w C) with w = 2 pi f.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used |H| = 1/(1 + w R C), adding the magnitudes
common_mistakes.why: R and 1/(wC) are in quadrature, so they combine as sqrt of squares.

criteria.text: Writes |H| = 1/sqrt(1 + (wRC)^2) or the equivalent complex divider

statement: In a first-order RC low-pass filter with R = 2.2 kΩ and C = 33 nF, at what frequency does the output lag the input by exactly 45 degrees? Answer in hertz.
solution: 1. The phase of the output is -atan(w R C), so -45 degrees occurs when w R C = 1. 2. w = 1/(R C) = 1/(2200 ohm * 33 nF) = 13770 rad/s. 3. f = w / (2 pi) = 2192 Hz.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reported w = 1/(RC) in rad/s as if it were hertz
common_mistakes.why: 1/(RC) is angular frequency; divide by 2 pi for hertz.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used C = 33 uF instead of 33 nF
common_mistakes.why: 33 nF is 33e-9 F; a factor of 1000 error in C gives a factor 1000 error in f.

criteria.text: States the 45 degree condition w R C = 1
Computes w from RC with correct nano scaling
Converts to hertz by dividing by 2 pi

statement: A 10 V peak, 500 Hz source is connected at node IN, and R1 = 50 Ω runs from IN to node A. Between A and ground there are two branches in parallel: a 5 µF capacitor, and R2 = 30 Ω in series with a 10 mH inductor. What is the peak voltage at node A, in volts?
solution: 1. w = 3142 rad/s. Capacitor branch: Zc = -j63.66 ohm. R-L branch: Zrl = 30 + j31.42 ohm. 2. Parallel combination: Zp = Zc Zrl/(Zc + Zrl) = 62.68 + j3.71 ohm (complex arithmetic). 3. Divider: vA = 10 * Zp/(R1 + Zp), |vA| = 5.569 V.

common_mistakes.mistake: Combined the branch impedance magnitudes as if they were resistances
common_mistakes.why: Reactances have different phase angles; magnitudes cannot be combined as resistors.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropped the R-L branch (capacitor only)
common_mistakes.why: The R-L branch is in parallel with the capacitor and changes the node impedance.

criteria.text: Gets Zc and Zrl as complex impedances
Combines the parallel branches with complex arithmetic
Applies the voltage divider and takes the magnitude

statement: The voltage across a 12 Ω heating element is v(t) = 5 + 10 sin(w t) volts. What average power does the element dissipate, in watts?
solution: 1. The DC and sine parts are at different frequencies, so their mean-square values add: Vrms^2 = 5^2 + 10^2/2 = 75 V^2. 2. Vrms = 8.66 V. 3. P = Vrms^2 / R = 75/12 = 6.25 W.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used the peak of the sum, (5 + 10)^2/R
common_mistakes.why: The sine is at its peak only briefly; average power uses its mean square, Vpk^2/2.

common_mistakes.mistake: Added the RMS values, (5 + 10/sqrt2)^2/R
common_mistakes.why: RMS values of components at different frequencies add in squares, not linearly (the cross term averages to zero).

criteria.text: Divides by R to get power

statement: What is the impedance magnitude, in ohms, of a 12 Ω resistor in parallel with a 25 mH inductor at 60 Hz?

common_mistakes.mistake: Added R and XL in quadrature, as for a series circuit
common_mistakes.why: That is the series impedance; in parallel the admittances add in quadrature.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used the resistor-style product over sum with magnitudes
common_mistakes.why: R and jXL are 90 degrees apart, so the sum in the denominator is a phasor sum.

criteria.text: Uses admittance (or complex parallel) rather than a scalar product-over-sum

statement: Find the resonant frequency, in hertz, of a series circuit with R = 8 Ω, L = 2 mH and C = 500 nF.
solution: 1. At resonance XL = XC, so w0 = 1/sqrt(L C) = 1/sqrt(2 mH * 500 nF) = 31620 rad/s. 2. f0 = w0/(2 pi) = 5033 Hz. The resistance does not affect f0.

common_mistakes.mistake: Gave w0 in rad/s as the frequency
common_mistakes.why: The 2 pi factor is needed to convert rad/s to hertz.

common_mistakes.mistake: Multiplied by 2 pi instead of dividing
common_mistakes.why: f = w/(2 pi), not w * 2 pi.

statement: What is the quality factor at resonance of a series RLC circuit with R = 8 Ω, L = 2 mH and C = 500 nF? Give it as a dimensionless number.
solution: 1. At resonance the reactance is X0 = w0 L = sqrt(L/C) = sqrt(2 mH/500 nF) = 63.25 ohm. 2. Q = X0/R = 63.25/8 = 7.906.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used the parallel-circuit formula R sqrt(C/L)
common_mistakes.why: In a series circuit Q = X0/R; R sqrt(C/L) is R/X0, which is the inverse and applies only to a parallel RLC with resistor across L and C.

criteria.text: Finds the reactance at resonance sqrt(L/C)
Uses Q = X0/R for series (not R/X0)

statement: A 5 kΩ resistor, an ideal 100 µH inductor and an ideal 2 nF capacitor are all connected across the same two nodes. Find the half-power bandwidth of this parallel circuit in kilohertz.
solution: 1. f0 = 1/(2 pi sqrt(L C)) = 355.9 kHz. 2. For a parallel RLC, Q = R sqrt(C/L) = 5000 * sqrt(2e-09/0.0001) = 22.36. 3. BW = f0/Q = 1/(2 pi R C) = 15.92 kHz.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used the series-circuit formula R/(2 pi L)
common_mistakes.why: That bandwidth belongs to a series RLC; for the parallel circuit BW = 1/(2 pi R C).

criteria.text: Uses the parallel Q = R sqrt(C/L)
Gets BW = f0/Q = 1/(2 pi R C)

statement: A series circuit with R = 8 Ω, L = 2 mH and C = 500 nF is driven at its resonant frequency by a 2 V RMS source. How large is the RMS voltage across the capacitor, in volts?
solution: 1. At resonance XL and XC cancel, so the current is limited by R only: I = 2/8 = 0.25 A. 2. XC = sqrt(L/C) = 63.25 ohm, so VC = I XC = 15.81 V. 3. Equivalently VC = Q Vs = 7.906 * 2 = 15.81 V, which is much larger than the source voltage.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assumed the capacitor voltage equals the source voltage
common_mistakes.why: Only the sum of the L and C voltages is zero at resonance; each is Q times the source.

common_mistakes.mistake: Multiplied by sqrt(2) as if converting to peak
common_mistakes.why: The source is RMS, so VC = Q Vs is also RMS; no conversion is needed.

criteria.text: Finds the current from Vs/R at resonance

statement: What capacitance, in picofarads, makes a tuned circuit with a 180 µH coil resonate at 1 MHz?

common_mistakes.mistake: Left out the 2 pi (used w0 = f0)
common_mistakes.why: w0 must be in rad/s, i.e. 2 pi f0.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used 2 pi only once: C = 1/(2 pi f0^2 L)
common_mistakes.why: The square applies to the whole angular frequency, (2 pi f0)^2.

criteria.text: Squares the full w0 in C = 1/(w0^2 L)

statement: A single-phase motor draws 3 kW at a power factor of 0.75 lagging from a 230 V RMS, 50 Hz supply. A capacitor across the supply is to bring the power factor up to 0.95, still lagging. What capacitance is needed, in microfarads?
solution: 1. Reactive power before: Q1 = P tan(acos 0.75) = 2646 var; after: Q2 = P tan(acos 0.95) = 986.1 var. 2. The capacitor must supply Qc = Q1 - Q2 = 1660 var. 3. Qc = w C V^2 gives C = 1660 / (2 pi 50 * 230^2) = 99.87 uF.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used f in place of w = 2 pi f
common_mistakes.why: The capacitor's reactive power is w C V^2 with w in rad/s.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used sin(phi) instead of tan(phi) for the reactive power
common_mistakes.why: Q = P tan(phi) when P is the real power; P sin(phi) would apply if P were the apparent power.

criteria.text: Computes reactive power before and after with P tan(phi)
Takes the difference as the capacitor's var
Uses C = Qc/(w V^2) with w = 2 pi f

statement: A load absorbs 4 kW of real power at a power factor of 0.8 lagging. What is its reactive power in kilovars?
solution: 1. S = P/pf = 4000/0.8 = 5000 VA. 2. Q = sqrt(S^2 - P^2) = sqrt(5000^2 - 4000^2) = 3000 var = 3 kvar (equivalently Q = P tan(acos 0.8)).

common_mistakes.mistake: Used P sin(phi), treating the real power as the apparent power
common_mistakes.why: sin(phi) times S gives Q; P is only the real part of S.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used P (1 - pf)
common_mistakes.why: (1 - pf) is not a ratio of any power-triangle sides.

criteria.text: Finds S = P/pf or uses tan(phi)
Gets Q from the power triangle

statement: A single-phase load takes 5.5 kW from a 230 V RMS supply at a power factor of 0.7 lagging. A capacitor in parallel brings the power factor to 0.95. By how many amperes does the line current drop?
solution: 1. I = P/(V pf). Before: 5500/(230*0.7) = 34.16 A. 2. After: 5500/(230*0.95) = 25.17 A (the real power is unchanged, the capacitor only removes reactive current). 3. Reduction = 34.16 - 25.17 = 8.99 A.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reported the new current instead of the drop
common_mistakes.why: The question asks for the reduction, I1 - I2.

common_mistakes.mistake: Took the drop in the reactive component of current only
common_mistakes.why: The line current is the phasor sum of real and reactive parts; its magnitude drops by less than the reactive part.

criteria.text: Uses I = P/(V pf) before and after

statement: A balanced three-phase load takes 90 kW in total at 0.8 power factor lagging from a 400 V line-to-line RMS, 50 Hz supply. The power factor is raised to 0.95 with three equal capacitors connected in delta across the lines. Find the capacitance of each capacitor, in microfarads.
solution: 1. Total reactive power to remove: Qc = P (tan(acos 0.8) - tan(acos 0.95)) = 90000 * (0.75 - 0.3287) = 37.92 kvar. 2. In a delta each capacitor sits across a line-to-line voltage of 400 V and supplies Qc/3 = 12.64 kvar. 3. C = (Qc/3) / (w V^2) = 12640 / (2 pi 50 * 400^2) = 251.5 uF.

common_mistakes.mistake: Did not divide Qc by 3 (or used the wye formula)
common_mistakes.why: A delta bank puts each capacitor across the full line voltage and shares Qc between three units; the same bank in wye needs three times the capacitance per unit.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used sin(phi) instead of tan(phi)
common_mistakes.why: Q = P tan(phi) for real power P.

criteria.text: Total Qc from P tan(phi) difference
Splits Qc over three capacitors and uses the line voltage for delta
C = Q/(w V^2) with w = 2 pi f

statement: Each phase of a balanced wye-connected load is 30 + j40 ohm. The load is fed from a balanced three-phase source at 400 V line-to-line RMS. What is the RMS line current, in amperes?
solution: 1. In a wye, each phase sees the phase voltage: Vph = 400/sqrt(3) = 230.9 V. 2. |Z| = sqrt(30^2 + 40^2) = 50 ohm. 3. The line current equals the phase current: I = 230.9/50 = 4.619 A.

common_mistakes.mistake: Applied the line voltage directly across one phase
common_mistakes.why: In a wye connection each phase gets only the line voltage divided by sqrt(3).

common_mistakes.mistake: Multiplied the current by 3 for the three phases
common_mistakes.why: Each line carries one phase's current; the factor 3 belongs to power, not to current.

criteria.text: Uses Vph = VL/sqrt(3) for a wye
States line current equals phase current for wye

statement: A balanced wye load of 30 + j40 ohm per phase is supplied at 400 V line-to-line RMS. Find the total real power it absorbs, in watts.
solution: 1. Phase current I = (VL/sqrt(3))/|Z| = 230.9/50 = 4.619 A. 2. Real power per phase = I^2 R = 21.33 * 30 = 640 W. 3. Total = 3 * 640 = 1920 W (check: S = 3 Vph I = 3200 VA, pf = 30/50 = 0.6).

common_mistakes.mistake: Reported the apparent power in VA as watts
common_mistakes.why: Only the resistive part dissipates power: multiply S by the power factor 0.6.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgot the factor 3 for three phases
common_mistakes.why: The total is the sum over all three phases.

common_mistakes.mistake: Put the full line voltage across each phase (delta-style)
common_mistakes.why: That is the delta result; a wye phase sees VL/sqrt(3).

criteria.text: Uses I^2 R (or S cos(phi)) for real power

statement: A balanced delta-connected load is 30 + j40 ohm per phase and is supplied at 400 V line-to-line RMS. What RMS line current does it draw, in amperes?
solution: 1. Each delta phase is connected across a line-to-line voltage: Iph = 400/50 = 8 A. 2. In a balanced delta the line current is sqrt(3) times the phase current: IL = 1.732 * 8 = 13.86 A.

common_mistakes.mistake: Gave the phase current as the line current
common_mistakes.why: In a delta, each line feeds two phases, so IL = sqrt(3) Iph.

criteria.text: Multiplies by sqrt(3) for the line current

statement: A balanced delta load of 60 + j45 ohm per phase is connected to a 208 V line-to-line RMS supply. Convert it to the equivalent wye load and use the single-phase equivalent circuit to find the RMS line current, in amperes.
solution: 1. A balanced delta equals a wye with one third of the impedance: Zy = (60 + j45)/3 = 20 + j15 ohm, |Zy| = 25 ohm. 2. The wye phase voltage is 208/sqrt(3) = 120.1 V. 3. IL = 120.1/25 = 4.804 A (same as sqrt(3)*208/75).

common_mistakes.mistake: Used the delta impedance as the wye impedance
common_mistakes.why: Delta to wye divides the impedance by 3 for a balanced load.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used the line voltage without dividing by sqrt(3)
common_mistakes.why: The wye equivalent works with phase voltage VL/sqrt(3).

criteria.text: Converts the delta load to wye by dividing by 3

statement: A balanced three-phase motor load draws 55 kW in total at 0.85 power factor lagging from a 415 V line-to-line RMS supply. Find the RMS line current in amperes.
solution: 1. For a balanced load P = sqrt(3) VL IL pf. 2. IL = P/(sqrt(3) VL pf) = 55000/(1.732 * 415 * 0.85) = 90.02 A.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used the single-phase formula P/(V pf)
common_mistakes.why: A three-phase load carries sqrt(3) times VL in the power expression.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used 3 instead of sqrt(3)
common_mistakes.why: P = 3 Vph Iph pf = sqrt(3) VL IL pf; the 3 goes with phase voltage, not line voltage.

criteria.text: Uses P = sqrt(3) VL IL pf

statement: A balanced three-phase source at 400 V line-to-line RMS feeds a balanced delta load through three identical line conductors of 0.5 + j1.0 ohm each. Each delta phase of the load is 45 + j24 ohm. What is the line-to-line RMS voltage at the load terminals, in volts?
solution: 1. Convert the delta load to wye: Zy = (45 + j24)/3 = 15 + j8 ohm. 2. Single-phase equivalent: source 230.9 V in series with the line 0.5 + j1.0 ohm and Zy. Total = 15.5 + j9 ohm, so I = 12.88 A. 3. Load phase (wye) voltage = I |Zy| = 12.88 * 17 = 219 V. 4. Line-to-line at the load = sqrt(3) * 219 = 379.4 V.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ignored the line impedance
common_mistakes.why: The feeder drops voltage; the load never sees the full source voltage.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used the delta phase impedance as the wye impedance in the per-phase circuit
common_mistakes.why: The single-phase equivalent requires the wye-equivalent impedance Zdelta/3.

criteria.text: Converts the delta load to wye before the per-phase analysis
Adds the line impedance in series as complex numbers
Converts the phase voltage back to line-to-line with sqrt(3)

statement: A transmission line has 12 Ω of series reactance. On a system base of 100 MVA (three-phase) and 66 kV line-to-line, what is this reactance in per unit?
solution: 1. Base impedance Zb = Vb^2/Sb = (66 kV)^2/100 MVA = 43.56 ohm. 2. Z(pu) = 12/43.56 = 0.2755 pu.

common_mistakes.mistake: Inverted the ratio (Zb/Z)
common_mistakes.why: Per-unit value is actual divided by base.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used the phase voltage (66/sqrt(3) kV) in Zb
common_mistakes.why: For a three-phase base, use line-to-line voltage with total three-phase VA; mixing phase voltage with total VA is inconsistent.

criteria.text: Computes Zb = Vb^2/Sb with consistent three-phase quantities

statement: A generator's subtransient reactance is 0.18 pu on its own base of 20 MVA and 13.2 kV. What is it on a system base of 100 MVA and 13.8 kV?
solution: 1. z_new = z_old * (S_new/S_old) * (V_old/V_new)^2. 2. S ratio = 5; voltage ratio squared = (13.2/13.8)^2 = 0.9149. 3. z_new = 0.18 * 5 * 0.9149 = 0.8234 pu.

common_mistakes.mistake: Left out the voltage correction
common_mistakes.why: The two voltage bases differ (13.2 kV vs 13.8 kV) and impedance base scales with V^2.

common_mistakes.mistake: Inverted the voltage ratio
common_mistakes.why: Impedance in pu goes with (V_old/V_new)^2: a larger new voltage base lowers the pu value.

common_mistakes.mistake: Inverted the power ratio
common_mistakes.why: A larger power base raises the pu impedance.

statement: A three-phase fault occurs on a 33 kV bus. The source, at 1.0 pu voltage, sits behind a generator reactance of 0.15 pu and a transformer reactance of 0.1 pu in series, both already on a base of 50 MVA and 33 kV. What is the three-phase fault current at the bus, in amperes?
solution: 1. Total reactance = 0.15 + 0.1 = 0.25 pu, so the fault current is 1.0/0.25 = 4 pu. 2. Base current Ib = Sb/(sqrt(3) Vb) = 50 MVA/(1.732 * 33 kV) = 874.8 A. 3. If = 4 * 874.8 = 3499 A.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used the single-phase base current S/V
common_mistakes.why: For three-phase quantities the base current is S/(sqrt(3) V).

common_mistakes.mistake: Added the reactances in parallel
common_mistakes.why: Generator and transformer are in the same path to the fault, so their reactances add.

criteria.text: Adds the series reactances in per unit

statement: The base values for a three-phase system are 100 MVA and 132 kV line-to-line. Find the base current in amperes.
solution: 1. Three-phase power is S = sqrt(3) V I with V line-to-line, so the base current is S_base/(sqrt(3) V_base). 2. I_base = 100 MVA/(1.732 * 132 kV) = 437.4 A.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used S/V (single-phase)
common_mistakes.why: The sqrt(3) comes from three-phase power S = sqrt(3) V I.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used S/(3 V)
common_mistakes.why: 3 V I applies to phase voltage; with a line-to-line base voltage the factor is sqrt(3).

statement: A 200 mV DC source drives the non-inverting input of an ideal op-amp. Rf = 33 kΩ goes from the output to the inverting input and Rg = 2.2 kΩ from the inverting input to ground. Assuming the output is not saturated, what is the output voltage in volts?
solution: 1. The inverting node follows the input, so Rg carries Vin/Rg and the same current flows through Rf. 2. Vout = Vin (1 + Rf/Rg) = 0.2 * (1 + 33000/2200) = 0.2 * 16 = 3.2 V.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used Rf/Rg without the 1
common_mistakes.why: The non-inverting gain is 1 + Rf/Rg; the 1 comes from the input voltage itself appearing at the output node.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used the inverting-amplifier result
common_mistakes.why: The input is on the non-inverting terminal, so the output has the same sign as the input.

criteria.text: Keeps the output in phase with the input

statement: An ideal inverting summing amplifier has its non-inverting input grounded and Rf = 20 kΩ in the feedback path. Three sources reach the inverting input through their own resistors: 800 mV through 4 kΩ, 1.5 V through 10 kΩ, and -200 mV through 2 kΩ. What is the output voltage, in volts?
solution: 1. The inverting node is a virtual ground, so each input contributes a current v/R, and their sum flows through Rf. 2. Input currents: 0.2 mA + 0.15 mA + (-0.1 mA) = 0.25 mA. 3. Vout = -Rf * sum = -20000 * 0.00025 = -5 V.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropped the minus sign of the inverting configuration
common_mistakes.why: The summing amplifier inverts: the output is the negative of the weighted sum.

criteria.text: Uses the virtual ground to get currents v/R

statement: An ideal op-amp is wired as a difference amplifier whose resistor ratios are not matched. Source v1 = 1 V feeds the inverting input through R1 = 10 kΩ, with R2 = 40 kΩ from the output back to the inverting input. Source v2 = 2 V feeds the non-inverting input through R3 = 20 kΩ, and R4 = 30 kΩ goes from the non-inverting input to ground. Find the output voltage in volts.
solution: 1. Non-inverting input voltage (divider R3/R4, no input current): v+ = 2.0 * 30000/(20000+30000) = 1.2 V. 2. The inverting node sits at v+. Superposition on the amplifier: Vout = v+ (1 + R2/R1) - v1 (R2/R1) = 1.2 * 5 - 1.0 * 4. 3. Vout = 6 - 4 = 2 V.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used the matched-resistor formula (R2/R1)(v2 - v1)
common_mistakes.why: That formula needs R4/R3 = R2/R1; here R4/R3 = 1.5 while R2/R1 = 4.

common_mistakes.mistake: Applied v2 directly to the non-inverting input, ignoring the R3/R4 divider
common_mistakes.why: The non-inverting input sees only v2 R4/(R3 + R4).

criteria.text: Finds v+ from the R3/R4 divider
Combines inverting and non-inverting gains for the output

statement: An inverting amplifier has Rin = 10 kΩ, Rf = 120 kΩ and a 1.5 V DC input. Its output can only swing between -10.5 V and +10.5 V. What is the output voltage, in volts?
solution: 1. Ideal linear gain = -Rf/Rin = -12, so the unclipped output would be -18 V. 2. That is beyond the negative limit of -10.5 V, so the output saturates. 3. Vout = -10.5 V.

common_mistakes.mistake: Gave the linear result without clipping
common_mistakes.why: The output cannot exceed the supply-limited swing; the ideal formula only holds in the linear region.

common_mistakes.mistake: Chose the positive rail
common_mistakes.why: A positive input to an inverting stage drives the output toward the negative rail.

criteria.text: Recognises saturation at the negative limit
Gets the sign of the rail right

statement: An ideal inverting amplifier with its non-inverting input grounded has R1 = 8 kΩ into the inverting input and a 50 kΩ feedback resistor Rf. It is driven by a 500 mV signal source that has 2 kΩ of internal series resistance. What is the output voltage, in volts?
solution: 1. The inverting input is a virtual ground, so the input current is Vs/(Rs + R1); the source resistance is in series with R1. 2. I = 0.5 V/(2000 + 8000 ohm) = 50 uA, and it all flows through Rf. 3. Vout = -I Rf = -50 uA * 50 kohm = -2.5 V.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ignored the source resistance
common_mistakes.why: The source's internal resistance adds to R1 in the input loop, reducing the gain.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used Rf/Rs as the gain
common_mistakes.why: The input resistor is Rs + R1 in total, not Rs alone.

criteria.text: Uses the virtual ground at the inverting input
Uses Rs + R1 as the input resistance

statement: Two ideal op-amp stages are cascaded. The first is non-inverting: the 100 mV DC input goes to its non-inverting input, Rf1 = 22 kΩ runs from its output to its inverting input, and Rg1 = 10 kΩ from that inverting input to ground. The second is inverting, with its non-inverting input grounded: the stage 1 output goes through Rin2 = 10 kΩ to its inverting input, and Rf2 = 47 kΩ is its feedback resistor. What is the final output voltage, in volts?
solution: 1. Stage 1 gain = 1 + Rf1/Rg1 = 3.2, so its output is 0.32 V. An ideal op-amp output is not loaded by the next stage. 2. Stage 2 gain = -Rf2/Rin2 = -4.7. 3. Vout = 0.32 * (-4.7) = -1.504 V.

common_mistakes.mistake: Added the two gains instead of multiplying
common_mistakes.why: Cascaded stage gains multiply because the first output is the second input.

common_mistakes.mistake: Used Rf1/Rg1 (no +1) for the non-inverting stage
common_mistakes.why: The non-inverting gain includes the 1.
